# Inset Panel Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

A floating panel over the whole main window, for work that needs more room than a popup and shouldn't disturb what is beneath it.

### Shape

#### Description

The panel floats over everything in the window, the ribbon and sidebar included, inset 32 pixels from every edge of the window. It has rounded corners, a border, and a shadow, and whatever it holds fills it. The window behind it is dimmed, and nothing behind it takes the mouse while it is open. Only one panel is open at a time.

#### Animating

The panel comes in each time it opens and goes away each time it closes with the [RiseInAnimation](../../animations/rise-in/RiseInAnimation.md): the panel is its surface, and the dimmed window around the panel is its dimming. Switching what the panel holds, such as opening a diff while the settings are open, swaps it in place.

#### Modal

While the panel is open, nothing beneath it can take focus or input; only the panel and what it holds can.
The mouse can't reach anything beneath: no clicks, scrolling, hovering, or tooltips, except that clicking the dimmed window closes the panel.
Focus moves into the panel when it opens and can't leave it. <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> cycle through what can be focused within the panel, going round from the last back to the first and the other way, rather than on to anything beneath. Anything that would move focus beneath while it is open, such as a task beneath finishing, sends focus back into the panel instead.
The main window's shortcuts that act on what is beneath do nothing while it is open: opening the palette with <Ctrl+P> (<Cmd+P> on macOS), and collapsing or expanding the ribbon with <Ctrl+F1> (<Cmd+F1> on macOS). Shortcuts that open something of their own, like the settings window, or quitting, still work.

#### Closing

The panel closes with a close or cancel button in what it holds, with <Escape>, or by clicking the dimmed window around it; clicking inside the panel never closes it. Once it closes, focus goes back to the chat input.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

content.content:
# Rise In Animation

## Concept

### Pitch

How something that floats over the window, holding the user's attention while it's there, comes in and goes away: rising gently into place over a dimming window, and sinking away again. Anything shown that way can use it.

### Shape

#### Description

Two parts move together: the surface, which is whatever comes in, and the dimming, which darkens everything behind it. Both follow one quick spring that settles in about a quarter of a second, from gone to fully in when coming in, and back when going away. Only how they look moves: where the surface settles, and so where it takes the mouse and focus, is its place from the start.

#### Coming In

The dimming darkens the window behind from not at all to 40% black. The surface fades in from transparent as it rises into place from about 28 pixels below, easing to a stop, as though tipping up towards the viewer. It comes in afresh each time what uses it opens.

#### Going Away

The same played backwards: the surface fades out as it sinks the same distance, and the dimming fades away. While it goes, neither takes the mouse nor focus, so what is beneath can be used straight away, and something opened meanwhile comes in as usual. Once the spring has had about a quarter of a second, it's gone.

#### Swapping

Changing what the surface holds while it's in swaps it in place without animating: only coming in and going away animate.

content.text:
Not me: everything I've done in this conversation has been read-only. But yes, the animation has been built, by one of your Code or Chain tasks. It's in your uncommitted changes, and as far as I can tell from reading the code it matches the spec. I haven't run the app or the tests to check.

**Where it is**
- `src/animations/rise_in.rs` is new and implements the RiseInAnimation spec.
- `src/inset_panel.rs` uses it (`inset_panel` for coming in, `closing_panel` for going away).
- `src/main_window.rs:556` (`render_panel`) keeps track of opening and closing.
- `spec/ui/animations/` is new, and `spec/ui/components/inset-panel/index.pi` is modified to reference it.

**Spec vs. code**
| Spec | Code |
|---|---|
| One quick spring, settles in about ¼ s | `SpringConfig::new(380., 38., 1.)` is almost critically damped (damping ratio about 0.97) and settles in about 0.2 s. `LEAVE_TIME` is 260 ms. |
| Window behind dims to 40% black | `DIM = 0.4` |
| Surface fades in and rises from about 28 px below | `DROP = px(28.)`; opacity and offset follow the spring |
| Only the look moves; mouse and focus areas stay put | The outer panel `div` stays at its inset position (and blocks clicks); only the inner surface moves |
| Comes in afresh each time it opens | the animation is keyed by `came_in`, which counts each open |
| Going away plays backwards and takes neither mouse nor focus | `closing_panel` has no click blocking or focus tracking, and its content isn't focusable |
| Something opened while one is closing comes in as usual | `Leaving::frame` drops the closing one as soon as something new shows |
| Swapping content doesn't animate | only a change from nothing to something counts as opening, so the key doesn't change |

A unit test covers the open, close and swap bookkeeping (`keeps_what_goes_away_until_it_has_gone`), and a main-window test checks that a closing panel doesn't take clicks and is gone once `LEAVE_TIME` passes (`src/main_window.rs:1327-1347`).

**One thing to watch:** while a panel is closing, `render_panel` asks for a new frame every frame for 260 ms. That redraws the main window, and because of the slow redraws I described earlier, the close may look choppier than the open. That's a general redraw-cost problem, not a problem in this animation.

**To confirm it yourself:** run `cargo test rise_in` and `cargo test inset_panel`, or just open and close Settings or a diff. I didn't run the tests because a build would use all your cores while the app and a task are running.
